results.title: Local Subnet vs. Public Egress
results.prompt: Explain whether an IP address of 192.168.1.50 is our public egress location or a private LAN subnet, and how you distinguish between the two.
results.reply:
That's a great question to kick things off! The address 192.168.1.50 is definitely part of a private LAN subnet, not your public egress location.

The easiest way to distinguish them is by looking at the reserved ranges defined by RFC 1918. Addresses starting with 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, or 172.16.x.x through 172.31.x.x are set aside specifically for internal networks. These aren't routable on the open internet, which is why your router uses Network Address Translation to swap that private ID for a unique public one whenever you're heading out to the web!

results.title: Platform Path & Binary Compatibility
results.prompt: We have a script targeting /var/run/docker.sock. Given that our host OS is Windows, explain how our Docker environment communicates with the host.
results.reply:
That's a classic architectural puzzle! Since we're running on Windows, your Docker environment isn't talking directly to a native Linux socket like it would on a standard distro. Instead, Docker Desktop creates a lightweight utility VM—usually powered by WSL2 or Hyper-V—to run the actual Docker Engine.

When your script tries to hit that socket, it's actually communicating through a proxy. Docker Desktop maps the `/var/run/docker.sock` path inside that Linux subsystem to a named pipe or a network port on your Windows host. So, while the script thinks it's talking to a local Unix domain socket, it’s really being routed into the backend VM where the daemon is actually listening!

results.title: Thermal Load & Throttling Inference
results.prompt: If system telemetry shows GPU temperature at 88°C and core clock drops from 2400MHz to 1100MHz under load, deduce the physical symptom and its effect on compile times.
results.reply: That's a classic case of thermal throttling! Your GPU is hitting its safety ceiling to prevent permanent hardware damage, which means those massive core clock drops are going to tank your throughput. You can expect your compile times to skyrocket because the hardware is intentionally choking its own performance to stay cool.
